title: A Little More Honest
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 24 of 40
content:
Greg arrived for the clinic appointment carrying an umbrella with one bent spoke and the expression of a man about to audition for a comedy show.

The waiting room smelled of floor cleaner and damp coats. Someone had taped a hand-drawn sign to the drinking fountain asking people not to leave cups in the sink. Through the window I could see Beach City traffic moving slowly around a puddle.

"Great day to get rained on by a medical professional," Greg said.

"We're indoors."

"Details."

He had made the appointment three times and canceled twice. Today he had asked me to accompany him, which was different from asking me to manage it.

"Do you want me at the desk with you?" I asked.

"No. I can do that."

He could. He gave the receptionist his information, checked the appointment time, and came back with a clipboard that looked strangely heavy in his hands.

"Everything okay?" I asked.

"Yeah. Just a lot of little boxes."

I glanced at the form.

"Would you like help reading any of it?"

He shook his head, then nodded.

"Maybe the one about emergency contacts."

"That's yours to choose."

He looked at me.

"I know. I just keep thinking whoever I write down gets assigned a whole job without being asked."

"Then ask them before you decide."

Greg sat beside me. He turned the form over and tried to call Steven, then stopped.

"He's got a lot going on."

"He can answer whether he wants to be listed. It's not the same thing as being on call every minute."

He made the call. Steven agreed, and Greg wrote his name with care. He asked whether I wanted to be an additional contact for visits when I was in Beach City. I told him yes, with the understanding that my travel through Lanternweald meant there would be times I wasn't reachable.

"Good," he said. "Two people, two actual choices."

The receptionist called his name.

At the doorway, Greg turned back.

"You'll still be here?"

"I'll be here when the appointment ends unless you tell me you'd rather go alone."

He smiled nervously and went inside.

I did not follow. The waiting room held a rack of old magazines and a potted plant whose leaves looked as tired as I felt. I watched an older man return a library book to the woman beside him and apologize for bending the cover. She shrugged and said she was more interested in whether he'd enjoyed it.

That seemed sensible.

When Greg came out, he was holding a card with a follow-up date.

"No apocalypse," he announced.

"That was never on the schedule."

"Then I'd like a refund for the suspense."

There was a shallow puddle across the direct path to the parking lot. Greg stepped toward it without looking, then caught himself when a woman using a walking stick asked the receptionist whether the side exit had a dry route.

The receptionist checked the weather notice.

"The front walk is safer today. The side path is being repaired."

Greg moved back to make room rather than insisting he could help her across the water. I waited beside him. The woman thanked the receptionist and made her own way out.

Afterward he looked at me.

"That was awkward."

"Why?"

"I almost did the whole heroic thing, and she hadn't asked for a hero."

"You're allowed to learn."

"I thought I was good at helping."

"You are. Sometimes you're so busy being ready that you forget to ask what the actual help is."

He considered that as we walked to the van.

I had wanted to fill every silence after the appointment with reassurance. Seeing him stop his own impulse reminded me to stop mine. We hadn't reached a verdict about his future, and a follow-up card didn't make me his guardian.

In the van he put the appointment papers into an envelope instead of leaving them on the dashboard where anyone passing could read them. He wrote the date on the outside.

"Look," he said. "Organized."

"Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late."

I laughed, and the tension finally eased.

We stepped under the awning. He looked relieved, but a little shaken.

"Do you want to tell me what they said?" I asked.

"Some of it. Not the whole thing."

"Okay."

He told me about a routine maintenance check, a recommendation to keep the follow-up appointment, and a few things he'd need to pay attention to. He didn't give me every private detail. I didn't ask for them.

Then he stared at the card.

"I nearly canceled again this morning."

"I know."

"How?"

"You checked your phone four times before we left."

He laughed.

"I guess I'm not subtle."

He leaned against the van.

"I can show up for Steven, for a friend, for somebody who needs a ride. But when it's something for me, I get scared it'll turn out expensive or complicated or that someone will tell me I've been doing everything wrong."

"Did anyone tell you that today?"

"No."

"Then perhaps the next appointment can be one thing on a calendar, not a verdict on your life."

Greg looked at the card again.

"You're annoyingly sensible."

"I get that a lot."

He held out his hand.

"Thanks for coming without taking over."

I took it.

"It mattered that you asked."

We drove to the shore and ate sandwiches inside the van while the rain cleared. Greg asked how my next visit to Moonroot was shaping up. I told him the archive had reorganized its public records so nobody needed to invent a reason to ask for a private appointment.

"Sounds like the kind of place that would love a clipboard."

"You have no idea."

He laughed.

We'd already talked honestly about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory. I was never going to be his only source of care, and he didn't have to be mine. Today had been a small example of what we meant: asking, answering, and not turning a favor into an invisible lifetime contract.

He reached across the console.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

The kiss was sweet and interrupted by the van's windshield wipers coming on unexpectedly. Greg looked at the switch as though it had betrayed him personally.

"Terrible timing."

"Very you."

We kissed again, a little slower.

At home he placed the follow-up card on the kitchen board, then moved it where he could see it without anyone else reading the details. I put the umbrellas by the door and made tea.

He sat beside me on the couch, warm and exhausted, and asked whether I would stay that evening.

"I'd like to."

The rest of the night remained private.

The next morning, Greg checked the date on the card and set a reminder himself. He didn't make me responsible for remembering.

He did ask whether I'd join him for breakfast.

I said yes.
